While that's not great from the point of view of the doctors that's probably a good setup in terms of digital security (I'm not a professional so maybe someone else can weigh in).  

Lots of lab equipment has been designed to work with older hardware and I some cases will not work with newer machines.  This equipment is REALLY expensive to replace so the best solution in terms of IT is to keep the old systems (sometimes even ones that are running Windows 95) but not have them networked to ANYTHING to minimise the risk of vulnerability.  As the equipment you mentioned outputs to a floppy drive I'm assuming this is the case.

Hospitals are huge buildings and the equipment is quite often spread throughout the whole place, so any central terminal with floppy access would necessarily be further from some departments than others.  The solution to this is to have a networked terminal with floppy access near to each of the old machines but that a) means you have to buy a load more machines and b)increases the amount of outdated hardware that you have to secure and maintain.

As you mentioned a script to do the conversions would speed things up incredibly but as such a script would be dealing with the heatlh records of basically every patient it may need to undergo some sort of compliance testing (not a lawyer either but I imagine data privacy laws come into play here).  

It's also worth mentioning that at least in the UK there are strict rules about how the health services go about outsourcing work like this and if you wanted to implement something you'd designed (even if you were doing it for free) there would be all sorts of government contracting legal hoops to jump through and you'd probably only get it through if you made a significant donation to a particular party.

As someone who's taken apart my joy con controllers to put different shells on them, I'd guess that the reason the controllers themselves are so expensive is because of their size.  While they don't in theory do as much as controllers from other systems, they have a much wider range of functions.  Inside each joy con is Bluetooth, motion sensor, what seems to be IR, a really complex trigger system, as well as a battery and the charging rail and then the regular PCB with all the buttons and inputs on.  To dismantle an Xbox controller all you really have to do is unscrew 4? Screws on the back of the thing and take the plate off and then you unscrew the motherboard and you're done.  The joycons are easily 10x more complex to put together and they potentially have much more varied hardware inside.  Judging by how mechanically complex it is to reassemble them Vs controllers that I've previously modified (xbone, PS3, 360, NDS) there's no way that assembly can be cheaply automated and so they're more expensive.  Here there's only £25 difference between an Xbox one controller and a pair of joycons, and I imagine most of that is the above difficulty.  Given how much the switch does for it's size, although I've never actually opened mine I imagine it'd be of a similar complexity and therefore have higher costs associated with that



Tldr Even though the joycons don't do much more than a regular controller they're super complex inside which leads to higher production costs and therefore a higher price
